title: SNAP family-4 max allotment FY2027
question: What will the first USDA FNS FY2027 maximum monthly SNAP allotment for a household of 4 in the 48 contiguous states and DC be, in dollars per month?
resolutionSource: USDA Food and Nutrition Service first official FY2027 SNAP Cost-of-Living Adjustments memorandum or table
resolutionRule: Resolve to the first official USDA FNS FY2027 SNAP Cost-of-Living Adjustments memorandum or table value for maximum monthly allotments, household size 4, 48 contiguous states and DC. The 2026-09-30 date is the catalog resolution deadline/latest-by date tied to FY2027 benefits becoming effective October 1, not a claim that publication occurs on that day. If USDA FNS posts the FY2027 table before 2026-09-30, that first official post controls. Use the dollar amount as first published, with no later revision or conversion.
drivers: Unobserved June 2026 Thrifty Food Plan cost is the mechanical basis
Food-at-home CPI running 2.7 percent year over year in May 2026
Annual FNS COLA table effective October 1
Low but nonzero policy-change risk around TFP rules

reasoning.result: Fetched BLS May 2026 CPI: all items +0.5 percent monthly and +4.2 percent year over year; food at home +0.1 percent monthly and +2.7 percent year over year; June 2026 CPI scheduled for July 14, 2026.

reasoning.result: Fetched ERS June 2026 forecast: food-at-home prices predicted +2.8 percent in 2026 with 95 percent prediction interval 1.4 to 4.4 percent; all food +3.2 percent with interval 2.2 to 4.2 percent.

reasoning.text: Base-rate/reference class: recent first-print household-of-4 values moved 939 to 973 to 975, and the local FY2026 anchor is 994. The year-to-year changes are about +3.6 percent, +0.2 percent, and +1.9 percent, with the current inflation evidence closer to the upper part of that recent range than to the FY2025 near-flat COLA.

Level, momentum, and mechanism: the best level anchor is the FY2026 catalog anchor of 994 dollars. Current grocery inflation has not collapsed; BLS shows 2.7 percent year-over-year food-at-home inflation in May 2026 and ERS puts 2026 food-at-home inflation at 2.8 percent. The eCFR rule makes this a mechanical TFP/June-cost update unless Congress or USDA changes the TFP basis before the FY2027 table.

Point: 994 dollars FY2026 anchor x 1.027 May food-at-home momentum = 1020.8, rounded to 1021 dollars. Interval: translate uncertainty around June 2026 TFP movement, publication rounding down to whole dollars, and modest policy/mechanical risk into about +0.6% to +6.1% from the 994 anchor, giving 994 x 1.006 = 1000 and 994 x 1.061 = 1055. This is wider than the ERS 1.4% to 4.4% food-at-home prediction interval because the resolver is the TFP basket, not CPI itself, and because policy or basket-specific food movements can add tail risk.

Catalog-prior reconciliation: the local prior point of 1010 and CI of 975 to 1045 looked too low after incorporating the 994 FY2026 anchor plus May 2026 food-at-home CPI at 2.7 percent and ERS 2026 food-at-home midpoint at 2.8 percent, so I shift the point up to 1021 and move the interval to 1000 to 1055 while keeping a similar uncertainty width.

Counter-consideration: below 1000 would require roughly less than +0.6 percent growth from the FY2026 anchor, plausibly from a sharp June 2026 TFP softening or a policy freeze/rebase. Above 1055 would require roughly more than +6.1 percent growth, plausibly from a fresh TFP reevaluation, commodity shock, or food-at-home spike several points above current CPI and ERS signals.

Review disposition: accepted the resolver clarification that 2026-09-30 is a catalog deadline/latest-by date, tightened the interval explanation around June 2026 TFP movement, rounding, and policy risk, and added reconciliation from the catalog prior to the updated 1021 point estimate.
